finding.claim: /transfer accepts negative amounts. The only check (line 11) is BAL[g.user] < amount, which passes for any negative amount. The sender's balance then increases and the recipient's decreases, so an authenticated user can steal from any account by sending a negative amount to it.

trace.note: amount read from attacker-controlled JSON, no type, sign or range validation
guard is only balance >= amount; for amount=-100 this is always true
sender balance decremented by -100, i.e. credited 100
recipient balance incremented by -100, i.e. debited 100

finding.guards_checked: Only the balance comparison at line 11. No amount <= 0 check on /transfer (unlike /withdraw line 21). No auth check on the sender beyond g.user, which is unset in this file.

verdict.guard_found: Only the balance comparison at bank.py:11 (BAL[g.user] < amount). It is a bare check whose result is used via abort(400), but it does not reject negative amounts. No sign check exists on /transfer, unlike the amount <= 0 check on /withdraw at bank.py:21. No auth decorator or before_request hook exists in the codebase (only bank.py is present), so g.user is set outside the code provided.
verdict.reason: All four trace lines match bank.py:10-14; for amount=-100 the guard at bank.py:11 is always false so the abort is skipped, BAL[g.user] (line 13) is credited and BAL[to] (line 14) is debited, and the only reachable precondition is a session that sets g.user, which this codebase does not show being restricted to anything above a normal user.

finding.claim: Non-finite JSON numbers bypass every comparison guard. Python's json module accepts NaN, Infinity and -Infinity by default, and Flask's request.json uses it. Sending amount=-Infinity to /transfer makes the sender's balance inf, after which /withdraw and /transfer checks (lines 11 and 21) always pass for finite amounts, allowing unlimited withdrawal. With NaN, every comparison is False, so the balance checks never abort.
finding.source: request.json["amount"] (bank.py:10 and bank.py:20), JSON body containing NaN or -Infinity
finding.sink: BAL mutation at bank.py:13, 14 and 23; guards at bank.py:11 and 21

trace.note: json parses -Infinity as a float, with no finiteness check
BAL < -inf is False, so the guard passes
with balance inf, 'BAL < amount' is False for any finite amount, so the guard passes

finding.guards_checked: Line 11 and line 21 comparisons only; no math.isfinite or type check. Behaviour follows from documented Python json semantics and was not executed, because the sandbox denied the verification command.

verdict.guard_found: none. bank.py:11 and bank.py:21 are plain comparisons whose results gate abort(400), with no math.isfinite or type check. The only other file in the directory is the skill tree, and no JSON parsing override, middleware, or before_request hook exists in bank.py. Flask's request.json goes through json.loads, which accepts NaN and Infinity by default.
verdict.reason: bank.py:10 takes amount from request.json with no finiteness check, so -Infinity passes the bank.py:11 guard (BAL < -inf is False), BAL becomes +inf at bank.py:13, and bank.py:21 then passes for any finite withdrawal at bank.py:23. The attacker must be an authenticated user, since g.user is set outside this file and not visible here. Nothing was executed, so the Python json behaviour is taken from documented semantics.

finding.claim: /transfer is not atomic. The sender is debited at line 13 before the recipient lookup at line 14. If 'to' is not an existing key, or is unhashable, line 14 raises KeyError or TypeError after the debit has been applied, so the sender loses funds and the 500 response does not roll back. This is a business-logic flaw that destroys funds rather than stealing them.

trace.note: 'to' read from attacker-controlled JSON with no existence or type check
BAL[to] raises KeyError for an unknown id or TypeError for a list or dict; no try/except or rollback

finding.guards_checked: Balance check at line 11 only. No recipient validation, no transaction or rollback.

verdict.guard_found: Only the sender balance check at bank.py:11 (abort(400)). No recipient existence or type check, no try/except, no transaction or rollback anywhere in bank.py. The sender is g.user, so the attacker can only reach their own funds; no other file in the directory adds middleware or guards.
verdict.reason: bank.py:13 debits BAL[g.user] before bank.py:14 performs BAL[to] += amount, and nothing between them validates `to` or rolls back, so an unknown or unhashable `to` (bank.py:9) raises KeyError or TypeError after the debit has been applied. Impact is limited to the authenticated caller's own balance (the sender is g.user), so this is a correctness and fund-loss bug, not theft; the claim's own wording says as much.

The "any caller acts as any user" outcome depends on an auth hook outside this directory that the candidate itself says it cannot verify, so it is not established by this code; the missing authentication is a design gap to flag, not a demonstrated vulnerability.

finding.claim: Check-then-act race (TOCTOU) on the balance. The balance check at line 21 and the debit at line 23 are not atomic. Flask runs threaded by default, so concurrent /withdraw or /transfer requests can all pass the check against the same balance and overdraw the account, driving it negative.
finding.source: Concurrent HTTP requests with the same g.user, attacker-controlled

trace.note: balance check reads BAL[g.user] without holding a lock
debit happens later in a separate step, so a concurrent request can pass the same check

finding.guards_checked: No threading.Lock, no atomic update, no per-account serialization. Exploitability depends on the deployment server's concurrency; the race is not reproduced here.

verdict.guard_found: none. No lock, atomic update, or per-account serialization in bank.py or anywhere else in the directory (bank.py is the only code file). The check at bank.py:21 is a bare comparison whose result gates abort(400) and nothing else. /transfer has the same unlocked check-then-debit at bank.py:11 and :13.
verdict.reason: The check at bank.py:21 and the debit at bank.py:23 are separated by a non-atomic read-modify-write on the shared BAL dict with no lock, so concurrent threads of one authenticated user's /withdraw (or /transfer at bank.py:11-13) can all pass the check and drive the balance negative; the only caveat is that exploitation requires a threaded server, which is not configured in this repo, and g.user is set outside this file.
